content: This document is an updated Cochrane Review, originally published in 2005 and previously updated in 2010, focusing on adjuvant antiviral therapy for recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP). RRP is a condition characterized by benign, wart-like growths in the upper airway, which can occur in both adults and children. These growths can lead to airway obstruction and changes in voice. The primary treatment for RRP typically involves repeated surgical removal of the papillomatous lesions. In addition to surgery, various agents, including antiviral medications, have been proposed as adjuvant therapies. These antivirals can be administered systemically or injected directly into the lesions. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of antiviral agents as adjuvant therapies in managing RRP in both children and adults. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, BIOSIS Previews, Cambridge Scientific Abstracts, and ICTRP. Both published and unpublished trials were considered, with the most recent search conducted on February 24, 2012. The inclusion criteria for this review were limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs). From the search, 143 references were identified, of which 43 were deemed appropriate for further assessment. Ultimately, only one RCT met the inclusion criteria. This trial involved 19 participants and was conducted at a single institution. The study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial investigating the use of intralesional cidofovir administered during surgical debulking. The participants included 15 adults and 4 children. The study was assessed to have a relatively low risk of bias. Over a 12-month trial period, no significant difference was observed between the group receiving intralesional cidofovir and the placebo group. Both groups demonstrated a significant reduction in the extent of disease, as measured during surgery using the Derkay Scoring System. However, there was no significant improvement in health-related quality of life in either group. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the use of antiviral agents as adjuvant therapy for RRP in children or adults. The included RCT did not demonstrate any advantage of intralesional cidofovir over placebo after 12 months. The study was limited by its small sample size and a mid-trial change in the concentration of cidofovir used. Initially, the concentration was 0.3 mg/ml for children and 0.75 mg/ml for adults, but this was later increased to 5 mg/ml for both groups. To definitively determine the effectiveness of intralesional cidofovir, a larger, adequately powered RCT using consistent, higher concentrations of cidofovir compared to placebo would be necessary. Future studies should also incorporate health-related quality of life and symptom-based outcome measures to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of treatment efficacy.
